Realty Income's Per-Share Earnings Test Takes Center Stage After KKR Deal and a Trimmed Price Target
sum: Realty Income closed a major European capital partnership and posted third-quarter numbers within days of each other this month — but the yardstick investors are watching is narrower than either headline. AFFO per share came in at $1.12 for the third quarter of 2026, up 3.7% year over year, the company reported on November 3. Net income attributable to common stockholders reached $403.9 million, or $0.43 per share, on quarterly revenue of $1.62 billion.

The per-share profit measure matters more than the size of any single transaction. A larger investment program would only reinforce the bullish case if AFFO per share keeps climbing alongside it; should that metric lag expectations, the deployment strategy would deserve a harder look.

Realty Income said on November 2 that KKR had committed EUR 528 million for a 49% equity interest in a European property portfolio. The assets span 54 retail and industrial properties across four European countries, giving the arrangement breadth across both multiple buildings and multiple markets — a detail that counts when judging whether the partnership can feed through to Realty Income's bottom line.

Roughly a week before the quarterly print, the company lifted its 2026 AFFO forecast to a range of $4.45 to $4.46 per share, up from $4.44 to $4.45 previously. Management also reaffirmed its $10.0 billion investment volume target for the year. That guidance band now serves as the next verifiable checkpoint, turning the growth thesis into a concrete expectation against which results will be measured.

On November 4, Freedom Broker lowered its price target on Realty Income to $63 from $69 while maintaining a buy recommendation. The two signals pull in different directions: the rating still endorses the company, while the lower target argues for more cautious valuation expectations. No rationale was disclosed for the cut, leaving investors to weigh whether earnings progress will justify the confirmed spending plans.

The distinction matters. A fundamentally positive view of the business and the level of valuation one is willing to pay are separate questions, and the risk of disappointment looms largest if expectations already price in a steeper earnings climb than Realty Income subsequently delivers.

Former India batter Cheteshwar Pujara has shared his predictions on the players and teams that could face major changes ahead of the IPL 2027 mini-auction. With the retention deadline approaching on November 17, franchises are working on their squad combinations for the next season.

In an interaction with Star Sports, Pujara discussed possible releases, captaincy changes and the teams that could enter the auction with the most work to do. He picked Kolkata Knight Riders as the teams likely to release the highest number of players, while backing defending champions Royal Challengers Bengaluru to retain their entire squad.

One of the biggest talking points is the future of two high-value players, Cameron Green and Nicholas Pooran. Green was bought by KKR for Rs 25.20 crore at the IPL 2026 auction, while Pooran was retained by Lucknow Super Giants for Rs 21 crore.
Pujara believes KKR could consider releasing Green despite the massive amount spent on him. However, he feels the franchise could attempt to bring the Australian back at the auction.
"They can still get him back at the auction," Pujara said while discussing KKR's options.

Pooran is another player whose future could be uncertain. The West Indies batter had a difficult IPL 2026 campaign, and LSG could consider releasing him to free up funds for the auction. Combination unites two innovative diagnostics platforms to build a first-of-its-kind connected point-of-need diagnostics platform

Sapphiros, a diagnostics platform backed by investment funds managed by KKR, and binx health, a point-of-care diagnostics company backed by Hildred, a health care-focused private equity firm, today announced that they have combined to form Onvaro, a next-generation diagnostics company built to bring fast, accurate, and affordable testing to the point of need across health care and consumer settings. As part of this combination, investment funds managed by KKR, through its Health Care Strategic Growth strategy, Hildred, and EQT Life Sciences are investing capital to support Onvaro’s growth trajectory.

Onvaro unites binx health’s established FDA-cleared, CLIA-waived platform and national commercial network with Sapphiros’ leading-edge technology, scalable development and manufacturing capabilities, and deep product pipeline. binx health’s commercial infrastructure gives new product innovations an immediate path to market, and Sapphiros’ proprietary printed electronics, blood collection technology, and retail pharmacy and strategic supply channels broaden the product portfolio and extend the reach of both companies’ products.

The combination creates a unique, diversified diagnostics company positioned for growth across retail, at-home, and other decentralized testing channels. Onvaro is also developing a first-of-its-kind connected diagnostics layer, which is designed to capture results at the point of testing and help efficiently connect patients with providers, telehealth platforms, pharmacies, and other care services.

sum: KKR manages nearly $800 billion in assets, yet its next big bet is a Phoenix company that fixes broken garage doors. The logic behind a $2 billion valuation reveals something unsettling about where private equity is hunting for returns.
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.

There is something almost funny about a firm that manages $796.49 billion in assets writing a check for a company that fixes garage doors. Yet that is reportedly what has happened. KKR has agreed to buy A1 Garage Door Service at a valuation of roughly $2 billion, adding a Phoenix operator founded in 2007 that took growth capital from Cortec Group in 2022 to a home-services portfolio that already includes Neighborly and Groundworks.
KKR (NYSE:KKR | KKR Price Prediction) is doing what the largest alternative managers have been doing for a decade: buying the cash flows that public markets cannot access directly.

A1 is a rollup of local garage-door repair and installation shops. The appeal is the demand pattern. A broken garage door is not a purchase a homeowner postpones or comparison shops for three weeks. The thesis rests on non-deferrable demand, local pricing power, and a customer who is not shopping on price when the technician arrives.

KKR is scaling this playbook. It already owns Neighborly, whose franchise brands cover plumbing, electrical, pest control, and HVAC, and Groundworks in foundation repair. The category is fragmented, unglamorous, and too small for public markets to price efficiently.

Private equity buys many small operators at low-single-digit multiples of earnings, consolidates back-office functions, and then sells the combined platform at a higher multiple. Multiple expansion does much of the work. It only works if the next buyer pays more, which is where the argument becomes uncomfortable.

Does KKR's $796B AUM Set the Stage for $1T Growth by 2030?
sum: KKR & Co. Inc.'s KKR expanding asset base underscores its evolution into a scaled and diversified global investment platform. With assets under management ("AUM") of $796 billion as of June 30, 2026, the company has already covered a substantial portion of the distance toward its $1-trillion AUM target by 2030. The breadth of its asset mix, along with acquisitions and expanding distribution capabilities, could help KKR sustain the momentum required to reach that milestone.

KKR's AUM spans Credit & Liquid Strategies, Private Equity, and Real Assets, reducing its dependence on traditional private equity for growth. Exposure to infrastructure, real estate, private credit, asset-based finance and insurance-linked investments provides multiple avenues to raise and deploy capital across market cycles. This diversification also supports a broader and more recurring management-fee base.

The company's long-term growth record reinforces the case for further expansion. Per its August 2026 Investor Presentation, KKR's AUM saw a compound annual growth rate ("CAGR") of 18% from 2010 through the second quarter of 2026. More importantly, management fees witnessed a 25% CAGR from 2020 through the second quarter of 2026, indicating that the increase in scale is translating into stronger recurring earnings power.

Strategic acquisitions are also helping KKR move closer to the $1-trillion mark. In May 2026, the company completed its acquisition of Arctos Partners, which enhanced KKR's sourcing and origination capabilities across private equity, credit, real assets, insurance and capital markets. In July 2025, KKR completed the acquisition of a majority stake in HealthCare Royalty Partners, a middle-market biopharma royalty acquisition company, adding nearly $3 billion to its AUM.

Nonetheless, the path to $1 trillion may not be completely smooth. Concerns surrounding private credit, weaker investor sentiment and rising redemptions across parts of the sector could moderately restrain near-term fundraising and AUM growth. Such pressures could become more meaningful if credit conditions deteriorate or institutional investors turn more cautious toward alternative assets.

There is no shortage of uncertainty in financial markets these days. The war in Iran has caused a spike in energy prices that has reverberated around the world and while prices have moderated somewhat, this may not last as global inventories continue to be drawn down at an accelerated pace. In addition, the build out of artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure has increased the demand for commodities and power and has also contributed to higher inflation. Currently, around one-third of U.S. Treasury Securities are owned by foreign countries. The persistent U.S. trade deficit helps to finance the increase in government debt. However, with greater onshoring and the repatriation of manufacturing capacity, there could be less demand for U.S. Treasury Securities in the future.

The U.S. recently intervened in the currency markets to support the Japanese Yen. It’s been almost 30 years since the U.S. has directly intervened in currency markets to support the Yen and highlights the extent the current administration will go to keep a lid on interest rates with midterm elections approaching.
Looking forward, higher inflation and lower demand for U.S. debt are significant catalysts that could continue to push U.S. interest rates higher and create a headwind for economic growth.

While it’s important to understand the fears in the markets, it is also important to recognize the opportunities and position yourself to benefit from the powerful long-term impacts of compounding. The high-profile bankruptcies of private credit borrowers First Brands and Tricolor late last year caused issues for private credit manager Blue Owl and raised concerns that a wave of defaults could hit the private credit sector. That has weighed on the share prices of Brookfield, Blackstone, and KKR, which have invested heavily in private credit. Both Blackstone and KKR are down about 43.5% from their 52-week highs, while Brookfield shares are off about 22%. I think the sell-off is a buying opportunity, which is why I've been loading up on these top financial stocks.

Banks have pulled back on lending over the years due to industry consolidation, increased regulation, and higher capital requirements. That has opened the door for non-bank financial companies to fill the gap by lending directly to companies. These private loans tend to be riskier, which is why banks aren't originating them. Default rates of private credit funds hit a record 9.2% last year, up from a record 8.1% in 2024. However, they have higher interest rates than other credit investments, compensating lenders for their higher risk profiles.

Several alternative investment managers have raised funds to grow their private credit portfolios. The industry currently has about $2 trillion in private credit AUM. That's double the level from 2020. Forecasters expect the private credit market to double again by 2030 to over $4 trillion in AUM.

The private credit situation could worsen, affecting Brookfield, KKR, and Blackstone. It has already had some impact on Blackstone, which manages a private credit fund open to individual investors (Blackstone Private Credit Fund or BCRED). sum: Global investment giant KKR is in talks to acquire a majority stake in Arctos Partners, the firm with minority stakes in roughly 20 pro sports franchises, including MLB, NBA, NHL, and NFL teams. On the surface, this deal would be stunning—but there are clear motivations for both sides.

On Friday, the Financial Times first reported that KKR and Arctos are in “advanced” discussions about a deal that could see the former become majority owner of the latter. A private-equity industry source confirmed to Front Office Sports that the two sides have been in talks since at least October. A representative for KKR declined to comment, and representatives for Arctos did not respond to requests for comment.
The ascendance of Arctos in the sports world has been sudden and sharp. A decade ago, the firm didn’t even exist; today, it has one of the most robust sports-focused portfolios in the industry.

Arctos owns minority stakes in the NBA’s Warriors, Jazz, and Kings; the NFL’s Chargers and Bills; the NHL’s Lightning, Mammoth, Wild, Penguins, and Devils (through an investment in Harris Blitzer Sports & Entertainment); and MLB’s Giants, Astros, Padres, Dodgers, and Red Sox (through an investment in Fenway Sports Group). It also owns stakes in the Professional Lacrosse League, college sports-focused firm Elevate, and soccer teams like Liverpool (through the Fenway Sports Group investment) and Paris Saint-Germain.

Why let someone else take control of this portfolio? When Ian Charles and Doc O’Connor formed Arctos in 2019, Charles was still bound by a five-year noncompete from his prior firm, Landmark Partners—which buys stakes in other investment funds—but the agreement did not cover sports, multiple sources familiar with the matter tell FOS.
“Working around the noncompete, sports was the opportunity,” one source says. “Charles and Doc teamed up and went to work.”
Now, Charles is free from the noncompete, and sources say O’Connor is moving toward a new phase of his career that includes spending much of his time living in Jackson Hole, Wyo.
